title: the pillar that's about money
hookLine: the pillar that's about money; 2.5% and why
carry: what you give purifies what you keep
tomorrow: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed

cards: Five pillars hold up a Muslim life. One is a statement of faith, one is prayer, one is fasting, one is a journey. And one is about a bank balance.

Not a general hope that people will be generous: a number, worked out once a year like a tax return, with a calculator or a pencil at the kitchen table. Mosques post online calculators for it. It can look like paperwork.
And its name means something close to purity.

teach.b: Zakat. Its root, z-k-w, holds two ideas at once: to be pure, and to grow. It's like pruning a plant.
You cut some away, and what's left is cleaner, and grows better.

teach.h: PRAYER AND ZAKAT, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: The Qur'an names prayer and zakat together again and again: “Establish worship, pay the poor-due.” God and neighbor in one breath. How does it work?

teach.h: TWO AND A HALF PERCENT, ONCE A YEAR.
teach.b: Once a lunar year, a Muslim whose savings stay above a set threshold, the nisab, traditionally measured in gold or silver, gives a share of that wealth.
The early rules set it, for silver, at a quarter of a tenth: one fortieth, two and a half percent. Not of income: of what you've held on to for a year. Why so small?
One way to read it: it's sized so anyone above the line can give it every year without being ruined by it, so it never stops. Where does it go?
The Qur'an names eight kinds of people, starting with the poor and the needy, and including people crushed by debt and the stranded traveler.
And it speaks of a known right in people's wealth for the one who asks and the one who goes without. So the money isn't framed as the giver's gift.
It's a right, already inside the wealth, being handed back. Shia practice adds khums, a fifth of the year's surplus. And beyond all of it is sadaqa, giving from the heart, any amount, anytime.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ counted even a smile at your brother as sadaqa.

how: Muslims whose savings are above the nisab threshold calculate zakat once a lunar year, usually 2.5 percent, and give it to people in the categories the Qur'an names, often through a mosque or charity; many time it for Ramadan.

games.q: what's inside the giving — tap the pairs.
p: giving from the heart, any amount
a fifth of surplus, in Shia practice

s: zakat is two and a half percent of your income
it's on savings held for a lunar year above the nisab, not on each paycheck.
in the Qur'an, zakat is often named right next to prayer
"Establish worship, pay the poor-due": prayer and zakat, side by side.
a hadith counts a smile as charity
even a smile at your brother is sadaqa (Tirmidhi).

games.q: a year has passed. your savings have stayed above the nisab the whole time. how much zakat is due?
o: one fortieth: two and a half percent.
games.why: one fortieth, two and a half percent: small enough that it can be given every year, so it never stops.

practice: Think about what you have right now. Not only money: time this week, food in the kitchen, a skill, a coat you haven't worn in two years. Let one thing come to mind that you've held on to longer than you need.
Picture the pruning: that one thing cut away and handed on. Notice how the rest of what you have feels after it. Lighter, or heavier?

wordCard.voice: Zakat. The third pillar: two and a half percent of savings, given once a year, from a root meaning to purify and to grow. Nineteenth word.

orig.note: Arabic: the third pillar, from z-k-w, to be pure and to grow.

carryVoice: Your line: what you give purifies what you keep. Like pruning: less, and it grows better. Day nineteen.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1454 (Abu Bakr's letter: a quarter of a tenth on silver)
